Black Monday

By: Kate Barry | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Farmers across the country unite against farm murders

Unique Selling Point:
On Monday Stellenbosch wine farmer Joubert Conradie was shot dead on his farm. His friend, Franschoek farm manager Chris Loubser recorded an emotional message on his phone pleading with farmers to wear black on Monday the 30th of October to show their support for the victims of farm murders, and a united appeal for assistance. The video has gone viral on social media and was followed by further videos calling for a tractor blockade of the N1 on Monday. Other farmers are walking the entire length of the N1 in a bis to draw international attention to this scourge.

Summary:
AfriForum released their statistics in April which claim that farmers are 4.5 times more likely to be murdered than other South Africans. The total amount of verified farm attacks for the 2016/2017 period is 357 and the amount of farm murders is a disturbing 74. 156 commercial farmers are killed per 100,000. According to the police’s annual crime statistics released on Tuesday‚ 34.1 South Africans are murdered per 100,000 of the population.

Further information:
Farm murders have drastically increased this year. So far there have been 66 murders inAfriForum and AgriSA have now called on all South Africans to wear black on Monday in support of the country's 34 000 farmers and to honor those who have been murdered.

Press Release:


Farm Attacks
Following two more fatal farm attacks in the Western Cape, thousands of farmers and members of
the public took to the streets – on what came to be known as Black Monday - to demand urgent
government intervention and an end to the killings. This year farm murders have been on the
increase and farmers say that the attacks are not treated as a priority crime. As tensions mount,
what are the solutions?

Script:


BLACK MONDAY

V/O: Last week thousands of South Africans gathered across the country – on highways, in fields, at work - to raise awareness around farm murders, and to honour those who have been victims of farm attacks.

Oscar: We are all experiencing high levels of crime and we need to tackle that, and each community needs to work with another community, black, pink, yellow, red… and we need to work together, we need to hold hands together to be able to deliver our country beyond this passage that we are going through.

V/O: This spontaneous protest, called Black Monday, was peaceful and strongly religious in nature with hundreds of people kneeling down to pray. But controversy erupted when a few protestors in Pretoria displayed the old South African flag.

Mbalula: The lawlessness, racist insurgency by hood rat racists who hijacked a serious civic topic for a racist political insurgency agenda, was open for all to see.

V/O: But some tweeters, including the Minister of Police, retweeted old photos dating back to 2010. Now Julius Malema has joined the fray.

Julius: “Let them announce the day they are coming back to Tshwane, let us meet them toe-to-toe, let us teach them who owns South Africa!”

Link: The ANC, EFF and several other organisations say that Black Monday was a racist campaign that elevated white above black lives. They claim that highlighting killings in one community, when 52 people are murdered each day in South Africa, is an expression of white supremacy.

V/O: There have been 74 farm murders this year, and victims were both Black and White. according to AfriForum’s Ernst Roets.

Ernst: When we say 74 murders, we not saying 74 commercial farmers have been murdered, we saying during these 350 odd attacks, 74 murders took place, this includes farm workers, it includes people who aren’t necessarily South Africans, it includes visitors, it includes families of the commercial farmer.

Calla: Actually, we as farmworkers, we don’t even know if we’re safe in our houses. And the reason I say that is, in the old days we had a good life. We could go wherever we wanted, but these days we can’t go wherever we want, because you don’t know where the danger is waiting for you. In South Africa, I think it’s reached the stage where we all have to stand together to put a stop to this.

V/O: Black Monday had its roots in a sudden wave of farm killings in the Western Cape. It began on the 14th of October, with the murder of Mark Fagan.

Joanne: We were hosting a birthday party, we had 7 young 14-year-old girls here.

V/O: Joanne Fagan lived here with her husband Mark, and their 14-year-old daughter Jamie. He ran a mobile petting zoo with dozens of rescued farm animals, which he took to children’s parties in Cape Town.

Joanne: At around midnight, my husband and I awoke to screams, with our children screaming and my husband flew out of bed, through the bedroom door, took him 2 strides and I dived for the safe to get our weapon. And as he opened the door, he just roared, like a bear, like a lion and there were 2 men right in front of him in balaclavas, attacking 2 of the birthday girls, while our daughter was on the stoep being attacked by 2 other chaps. And, as my husband pushed and shoved these 2 men out of the house, keeping us safe, there was a gunshot and it hit him fatally in his heart, I was literally 2 or 4 strides behind him with the weapon but as I came around the corner they were gone.
And I just crouched down like that and I said “We love you Markie, we love you Markie, everything’s alright.” While I was trying to secure the area. I honestly didn’t know he was fatally shot until I rolled him over.”

Link: A smallholding on this secure rural estate, just outside Philadelphia is where Mark Fagan was murdered. It is monitored 24 hours by cameras, it is patrolled by the neighbourhood watch, and has controlled access. But, like so many farms across the country, it is isolated and vulnerable.

V/O: According to official crime stats the murder rate in South Africa is 34 per hundred thousand people. For the police service, it’s higher: 52 per hundred thousand. But for farmers it’s 156 per hundred thousand. Farmers are four-and-a-half times more likely to be murdered than ordinary citizens.

Link: One of the slogans of the Black Monday campaign was “No Farmers, No Food”, or wine for that matter. But let’s look at the stats. Agriculture grew its production by more than 30% this year, one of two sectors that showed any growth at all. Farming, almost single-handedly, has pulled this country out of recession.

Johan: Fact is, if the shops shelves run empty at some stage, we’ll ask the question “Where are our farmers?”.

V/O: Johan Burger is an independent crime analyst.

Johan: Everybody on farms are either victims or potential victims of farm attacks, and it should not be treated as a racial issue. It should not be treated as a white only problem. It is everybody’s problem.

Chris: For me, today is not about black or white. It’s about the country’s farmers. It doesn’t matter what colour or race you are.

V/O: Ten days after Mark Fagan was killed, another senseless murder occurred in the Western Cape. 47-year-old father of two, Joubert Conradie, was shot in the kitchen of his Stellenbosch wine farm. The perpetrator climbed through the bedroom window of 15-year-old Hannes, who was away at boarding school.

Marlene: My husband Joubert got up and he heard a noise. He didn’t say anything, he just left me to sleep, but I did wake up immediately.

V/O: Marlene Conradie and 11-year-old Jana were at home.

Marlene: He took the gun and he ran down the hallway, and it was in seconds that I heard many shots. I pressed the panic button, and then he came around the corner, and took the wall and he said “I’ve been shot”, and there was blood streaming over him. There was blood everywhere in the house. I was running in my pyjamas, I slipped in his blood.


V/O: The next day a neighbouring farmer, Chris Loubser sent an emotional video to his friends on What’s App.

Video: You feel so powerless, and you feel must do something to help the country’s farmers. Come, let’s wear black on Monday – I’ve got an old, black T-shirt in the cupboard – so we can just show a little respect to those farmers who have lost their lives this year.

V/O: The video struck a chord and went viral on social media. Black Monday dawned in Stellenbosch with crowds gathering in a field near the Conradie’s farm.

John: When you pushed Send on that message, did you think this would be the result?

Chris: No, no, I didn’t know my 20 friends had so many friends!

V/O: People came from all over the Western Cape, to protest against farm attacks. The procession was meant to leave for Cape Town at 6:00am, but more and more supporters kept arriving.

Brandon: We’re actually from Somerset West. We are a construction company and we just came out as a group to show our support I’m married and I have children. If this happened to my children how would I feel?

V/O: Led by a team of black horses, the Black Monday protestors finally made their way towards the N1. Support along the road was visible, giving an indication of how united this community is against crime.

Sfx: “Genoeg is genoeg!”

V/O: The convoy was so enormous, that it took them over 4 hours to reach the City. Similar protests were held in Oudtshoorn, Vryburg, Tzaneen, George, Johannesburg, Brits, New Zealand, Perth, Melbourne and even South Dakota, in the USA.

Sfx: Truck hooting

Dan: This was just civil society just claiming their right to protest. And of course, we do have a right to protest, and we should protest when people close to us, and friends and family are murdered. Every South African has that right.

V/O: Dan Kriek is Deputy President of AgriSA which represents 28 000 commercial farmers, and 100 000 emerging farmers.

Dan: What do farmers want? We want a police station, we want police offices that are well-trained, we want a police station that is well-resourced, we want good service levels and we want good relationships, and we want their investigative work to be of such a high quality that we can take the cases to court. That is what farmers want.

Link: Our attempts to secure an interview with the Police Minister and the Western Cape Police Commissioner were unsuccessful.

V/O: The sector employs 900 000 people, but since Black Monday, there have been 4 more farm murders.

Marlene: In this moment, we must spread love in South Africa and to the rest of the world. This world can only be saved with love and not hate. It’s my plea to the highest government in this country to help and to step in.
